ACIV: Value stocks outside the US, picked by an active process hunting underpriced companies across developed and emerging markets, with industrials the biggest slice. It aims to catch value abroad that plain indexes miss, accepting currency swings and a mix that can look quite different from foreign benchmarks.
ATCL: Exposure to synthetic autocallable notes through an index of them, notes that pay income while the underlying stocks cooperate and can be called away early when they rise. The income is the draw; the hidden risk is steep losses if stocks fall past the notes' barriers.
AVGW: A single stock strategy built on Broadcom, the chip and software giant, using swaps for extra exposure plus an options program aiming to pay distributions weekly. It amplifies one popular semiconductor stock's moves and converts some of them into income, a concentrated and volatile ride.
CARZ: Companies building the future of vehicles: electric car makers, self driving technology, battery and parts suppliers, with technology about two thirds of the fund. It is a focused bet on the car industry's reinvention, swinging with auto cycles and tech sentiment alike.
CBSE: Small and mid sized companies from around the world picked for strong finances, low prices or growth potential, currently heavy in technology and energy. Active stock picking drives everything here, so it can look very different from global indexes and swing with its concentrated bets.
CLOO: The safest layers of collateralized loan obligations: investment grade debt issued by vehicles that bundle corporate loans together. It pays more than comparable plain bonds because of the structure's complexity, while sticking to the top rated slices where losses arrive last.
CPSA: Options on the S&P 500 set up each August for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
CPSJ: Options on the S&P 500 set up each July for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
CSIO: Infrastructure companies worldwide: utilities are over half, with transportation, energy and communications networks behind, all businesses owning essential physical systems. It targets income and steady growth from tolls, bills and fees people pay regardless of the economy, actively hunting opportunities across borders.
DRUP: Large Nasdaq listed companies picked as disruptors, technology over half with health care innovators and media platforms behind. It concentrates on firms shaking up their industries, so it is a growth bet with bigger swings than a broad tech fund.
EVPF: Preferred securities and other income producers: the hybrid shares companies issue that pay steady dividends ahead of common stock, plus bonds, at home and abroad. It targets a higher income stream than plain bonds, sitting between stocks and bonds in risk and behavior.
GABF: Financial services companies of all sizes: banks, insurers, asset managers, payment firms and brokers, nearly nine tenths of the fund. It is a focused bet on the money business, so it rises and falls with lending, markets and deal making.
GMNY: New York municipal bonds, debt from the state, its cities, transit systems, schools and other public projects, paying interest exempt from federal tax and usually New York state tax too. It is a tax smart income holding for New Yorkers, concentrated in one state's finances by design.
GMOD: A balanced portfolio that shifts among stocks, bonds and alternative strategies worldwide, run as a fund of funds by a famously valuation driven shop. It aims for steady long term growth with smaller drops than a pure stock fund, adjusting its mix as values change.
GXPD: The full consumer discretionary sector in one fund: retailers, carmakers, restaurants, travel and media companies that depend on households having money to spare. It takes the sector at full market weight, giants and all, so it rides consumer confidence and spending cycles directly.
HXA: An arbitrage fund that trades around corporate events like mergers, restructurings and corporate spinoffs, using stocks, closed end funds, warrants and derivatives where the deals are. Most of the money waits in money market instruments between opportunities, so it aims for steady, deal driven gains rather than market returns.
HYIN: Listed vehicles that hold private credit and other alternative income assets: business development companies and closed end funds that lend to private businesses. It offers a doorway into private lending income through the stock market, with share price discounts and credit risk riding along.
IBIL: Inflation protected US Treasury bonds that all mature around 2035, packaged like a single TIPS bond with a known end date. Its payments and principal adjust with inflation until then, suiting savers protecting a future expense from rising prices, though market prices still swing with real interest rates.
JFLI: Income from everywhere: dividend stocks, bonds and convertible securities across the US and the world, blended flexibly by the manager as opportunities shift. It aims to pay steady income from many sources at once, so no single market's bad year decides its fate.
JULB: Options on a large US stock fund in a structured outcome design that starts each July, absorbing a slice of losses over its outcome period in exchange for capped gains. It offers stock exposure with a planned cushion, suiting investors who prefer knowing the trade off in advance.
KMAY: Options on a small company stock fund, set each May for a one year outcome period that absorbs a slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. Small caps swing harder than large ones, so the cushion is the appeal, paid for by missing the biggest small stock rallies.
LSCP: A core plus bond portfolio run dynamically by a veteran bond team: government, corporate and mortgage bonds of any maturity, with its interest rate stance kept near the broad bond market's. The active tilts aim to add return over a plain core fund, for better or worse.
MDLV: Large US companies that pay dividends and look cheaply priced, chosen by a small boutique manager across banks, industry, energy, utilities and more. It is an old fashioned value and income holding, favoring cash paying stalwarts over growth stories.
MINN: Minnesota municipal bonds, debt from the state's cities, schools, hospitals and public projects, paying interest exempt from both federal and Minnesota state taxes. It is a hometown income holding for Minnesota residents, with the tax benefit worth most to those in high tax brackets.
MSTI: Short term bonds for strategic income: a mix of government, corporate and other bonds kept on short maturities to limit interest rate swings. It aims to pay more than cash and money market funds while keeping price moves modest, a cautious step up in yield.
MYCJ: Corporate bonds that all come due in 2030, packaged like a single company bond with a known end date, paying interest until the bonds mature. It suits savers matching money to a goal around 2030, and its price swings fade as the date approaches.
NBET: Companies driving the energy transition and rebuilding infrastructure: traditional energy firms cutting carbon, clean power builders, and grid and pipeline operators, mostly energy with some utilities. It bets on the decades long shift in how the world makes and moves energy, with commodity swings along the way.
NDIA: Indian companies picked actively, led by banks and other financial firms with consumer, industrial and energy names behind, all in one fast growing economy. It is a single country growth bet, so it swings with India's markets, politics and currency.
NETL: Net lease real estate companies, landlords whose tenants sign long leases and pay the taxes, insurance and upkeep on top of rent. Those leases make income steadier than most property stocks, so it is a defensive corner of real estate, still sensitive to interest rates.
NQLT: Mid and large sized companies chosen for quality: strong finances, reliable profits and durable businesses, spread across technology, consumer, financial and health care names. It is a plain spoken core stock holding that favors proven operators over speculative growers, at home and some abroad.
NTSD: Large US stocks held directly, with international stock futures layered on top so each dollar carries both home and foreign exposure. The stacked design aims to squeeze more diversification from the same money, and the leverage means losses can outrun a plain global fund.
PBOC: Options on the S&P 500 set each October for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is a known cushion for the year, paid for by giving up strong rallies in large US stocks.
PBSE: Options on the S&P 500 set each September for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is a known cushion for the year, paid for by giving up strong rallies in large US stocks.
PLGI: A tactical mix of growth stocks and income producing securities and options, traded actively and often as the manager shifts between offense and income. The flexibility is the point: it can chase growth or lean on payouts, and results depend entirely on the manager's timing.
PSCQ: Options on the S&P 500 in a conservative structured outcome design starting each October, cushioning losses while keeping only part of any gains. The conservative tilt favors protection over participation, suiting investors who want stock exposure on a leash.
PUI: Utility companies chosen by momentum: at least thirty power, gas and water providers showing the strongest recent price trends, rebalanced as leadership rotates. Chasing the hottest names in a normally sleepy sector makes it livelier than a plain utilities fund, for better or worse.
QIS: A bundle of outside quantitative trading strategies, accessed through swaps, spanning stocks, interest rates, commodities and currencies all at once. It aims for hedge fund like returns that move independently of a normal portfolio, with layers of strategies most investors could not reach directly.
ROSC: Small US companies screened by several factors at once, quality, value and momentum signals blended to manage the risks small caps carry. The multifactor approach aims to smooth the small cap ride, though it can trail simple small cap funds when one factor runs hot.
SEMY: An income strategy built on options tied to a leveraged semiconductor fund, collecting premiums from the chip sector's big price swings to fund payouts. It doubles down on volatility: a leveraged underlying plus options means sharp moves both ways, with gains capped by design.
SRHR: Real estate investment trusts plus covered calls sold on those holdings, turning rent backed dividends and option premiums into a higher income stream. It gives up part of any REIT rally to pay that income, and it still falls when property stocks drop.
TDSB: A cautious allocation across stocks, bonds, real estate and other asset classes, managed to keep its overall risk near a set target rather than chase returns. It is built to participate modestly in good times and protect in bad ones, suiting investors who prize a smoother path.
TEMD: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies, in dollars and in local currencies, paying higher interest to compensate for political and currency risk. It is an income holding from the developing world, actively managed, that swings more than rich country bond funds.
TENJ: Options on large US stocks set each June for a twelve month outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. The buffer is the design target for each period, and the terms restart every June for the next round.
TILL: Agricultural commodity futures: corn, wheat, soybeans, livestock, sugar and other farm goods, traded actively rather than held to a fixed recipe. It packages farm price exposure without a K-1 tax form, and it swings with weather, harvests and food prices worldwide.
TOLL: Companies that dominate their markets: monopolies and near monopolies with pricing power, measured by how concentrated their industries are, across technology, finance, industry and health care. The idea is that dominant firms defend profits better, making this a quality tilted bet on market leaders.
TRBF: A bond portfolio concentrated in mortgage related debt: home and commercial mortgage securities from government agencies and private issuers, plus mortgage loans. That concentration is its identity, aiming for mortgage market income with active management, and it lives and dies by housing and property credit.
USL: Crude oil futures spread evenly across the next twelve months of contracts, rather than betting everything on the nearest month's price. Spreading the contracts softens the cost of rolling futures each month, though it still moves with oil prices and is a trading tool, not a long term holding.
VDG: Growth companies in developed markets outside the US: Europe, Japan, Canada, Australia and their peers, led by banks, technology and industrial firms screened for growth traits. It offers the growth half of foreign investing, complementing value funds abroad, with currency swings included.
XFLX: A flexible fund of bond funds, spreading money across other ETFs that hold government, corporate and mortgage bonds of varying maturities and quality. The manager shifts the blend as conditions change, aiming for income with managed risk rather than a fixed bond recipe.
XRLX: A conservative fund of funds, mixing core stock ETFs with a solid base of bond ETFs and adjusting the blend as conditions change. It aims for modest growth with limited drama, suiting cautious investors who want one holding that leans defensive by default.
